issue.issue_text: Challenge to the conviction of the appellant.

facts: The appellant was convicted by the Special Judge, CBI, under Section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 13(2) read with Section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption (P.C.) Act.
The conviction was based on the testimony of 23 witnesses and documentary evidence presented by the CBI.
The appellant was sentenced to three years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine.
On a prior appeal, the High Court had already affirmed the conviction and sentence.
The appellant's counsel argued before the Supreme Court that the appellant was unnecessarily targeted and the sentence was harsh.
law: The Court noted the legal standard that for a conviction under Section 120-B IPC and Section 13(1)(d)(ii) of the P.C. Act, there must be supporting evidence.
application: The Supreme Court carefully considered the arguments advanced by the appellant's counsel.
The Court also conducted its own review by perusing the evidence, the documents available on record, and the judgment of the High Court that was being challenged.
reasoning.conclusion: After reviewing the evidence and the prior judgments of both the Trial Court and the High Court which had already affirmed the conviction, the Supreme Court rejected the challenge to the appellant's conviction.

issue.issue_text: Challenge to the quantum of sentence imposed on the appellant.

facts: The criminal offense occurred in 1994, approximately 23 years before the Supreme Court's judgment.
The appellant (the then Deputy CEO) had the improperly allotted plot cancelled by the authority (NOIDA).
The appellant unconditionally surrendered the plot and offered to forgo the refund of the money he had deposited for it.
The conviction put the appellants' service and retirement benefits in jeopardy.
law: The Court has the discretion to determine an appropriate sentence based on the specific facts and circumstances of a case.
The original conviction was under Section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code and Section 13(2) read with Section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
application: The Supreme Court considered several mitigating factors in its decision to reduce the sentence.
It took into account the significant passage of time (23 years) since the commission of the offense.

The Court noted the appellant's actions after the offense, specifically that he had surrendered the plot and was willing to lose the money he had paid, which negated the pecuniary advantage gained from the crime.
The Court also considered the severe collateral consequences of the conviction, such as the loss of the appellants' jobs and retirement benefits.
Weighing these specific circumstances, the Court determined that the original three-year sentence was too harsh.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the challenge to the quantum of the sentence. Considering the long delay since the offense, the appellant's surrender of the plot, and the jeopardy to his service benefits, the Court reduced the sentence of imprisonment for both appellants from three years to two years.

arguments.issue_text: Challenge to the conviction of the appellant.
appellant_arguments: The appellant acted in the course of their official duty based on notes put up by the office.
There is no evidence to prove that the appellant agreed to do any illegal act.
No dishonest intention can be attributed to the appellant's actions.
The lower courts erred in convicting the appellant for criminal conspiracy.
respondent_arguments: The lower courts correctly convicted the appellants for conspiracy in the illegal and arbitrary allotment of plots.
The appellants abused their position as public servants to gain pecuniary advantage for themselves and their kith and kin.
The alteration of plots and manipulation of records to their own advantage establishes a prior concert and dishonest intention.
The co-accused were associated in every aspect of the events, which proves the charge of conspiracy.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: To establish a charge of conspiracy, knowledge about indulgence in either an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means is necessary.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court upheld the conviction based on the concurrent findings of the lower courts, concluding that the appellants acted in clear abuse of their position. The alteration of a plot from 'guest house' to 'residential' and its subsequent allotment to one of the appellants, in violation of norms and with undue haste, was not a legitimate official act but a criminal conspiracy manifesting a dishonest intention to gain a pecuniary advantage and gratify private interest over the public interest they were entrusted to protect.
legal_tests_applied: To establish a charge of conspiracy, knowledge about indulgence in either an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means is necessary.
In case an authority proceeds in undue haste, the Court may draw an adverse inference from such conduct.
A public servant is culpable if, while holding office, they obtain for any person any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage without any public interest.
why_appellant_lost: The court deferred to the concurrent findings of the trial court and the High Court, which it found to be 'well balanced' and saw no reason to interfere with.

The alteration of the plots with the dishonest intention of the appellants gaining pecuniary advantage to themselves in altering the plots to their own advantage establishes prior concert of the appellants in manipulating the maps/records to suit their convenience.
The undue haste shown at every stage leads to an inference of abuse of position and arbitrariness and also the conspiracy.
The co-accused appellant was associated in each and every aspect of these events which clearly bring home the charge of conspiracy of both the accused.
why_respondent_won: The lower courts' concurrent findings that the appellants acted in clear abuse of position to gain pecuniary advantage were upheld as well-balanced.
The evidence of altering plots and manipulating records was sufficient to establish a prior concert and dishonest intention, proving the conspiracy charge.

The court accepted that the appellants' actions, specifically the alterations to the site plan, reflected nothing but a dishonest intention to gratify their private interest instead of the public interest.
The association of the co-accused in every aspect of the events was sufficient to prove the charge of conspiracy.
policy_considerations: Power vested by the State in a Public Authority should be viewed as a trust coupled with duty to be exercised in larger public and social interest.
Public Authorities cannot play fast and loose with the powers vested in them.

An Authority is under a legal obligation to exercise the power reasonably and in good faith to effectuate the purpose for which power stood conferred. In this context, 'in good faith' means 'for legitimate reasons'.
